intro_en: "The mountain that is green all year round..." The Israel National Trail crosses the Carmel ridge, among green trees and with spectacular lookouts over Haifa Bay and the Carmel coast.
character_en: (For those walking from the north) The segment is characterised by ascents and descents, some of them fairly steep. The lookouts over the bay and the Carmel coast are spectacular, and thanks to the natural woodland and planted forest, parts of which are recovering from the fires, the trail is shaded along many sections.
shortcuts_en: The route is modular and can be divided into short sections.
transport_en: Kibbutz Yagur and Oren Junction on Road 4
pois_en: Scenic lookouts over the Carmel, the Carmel coast and the valley. Rich Mediterranean woodland. Nahal Heik. Yishah Caves.
important_en: At the end of the segment, on the descent to the Nahal Oren parking area, there is a short section descending a rocky cliff.
Some of the descents are a little steep and are not suitable for walking when the route is muddy.
description_en:
We set out from the hikers' parking area on the edge of Kibbutz Yagur, which sits right on the seam between Mount Carmel and the valley. We walk a little way south along the road that encircles the kibbutz, until a right turn towards the Carmel and the start of the climb up the mountain.
The path is narrow and winds like a snake among the woodland trees, carrying us in relative comfort up the mountain. The section of trail between Yagur and Isfiya has a name, the Ma'apilim (Illegal Immigrants) Trail: this is the route along which the illegal immigrants who escaped from the Atlit detention camp in 1945 came down from the Carmel to Kibbutz Yagur. The trail crosses the "Carmel Scenic Road", a dirt road for vehicles. Immediately after it there is a hikers' picnic area, a recommended spot for a break and a rest.
After a short walk, the trail climbs along dirt roads up to the entrance to the village of Isfiya. Shortly before it, we pass the David Eisen Lookout memorial site. The final section of the climb is on sand, between the houses of the village.
Crossing the road also means crossing the "watershed line", the crest of the Carmel and the highest point of this segment, about 520 metres above sea level.
From here we begin the descent down the other side of the Carmel. We march along a dirt road parallel to the channel of Nahal Heik, and after a short stretch we enter the area damaged in the great fire of 2010; here we can see the recovery of the woodland and forest that were badly hit in the fire.
We walk the final section of Nahal Heik in the stream bed itself, a beautiful stretch of the stream, which cuts into hard limestone and forms a short canyon. Iron railings have been installed to help where needed.
Leaving the channel onto a dirt road marks our arrival at Alon Valley (Bik'at Alon), at whose centre runs the channel of Nahal Oren. The trail crosses Nahal Oren and the valley and climbs Har Shokef, within a gully that drains the slopes of Har Shokef into Nahal Oren. On this section the trail is marked black. Shortly after the trail leaves the gully onto a dirt road, we follow the black trail to a meeting with a red trail that leads us to the summit of Har Shokef.
From the summit of Har Shokef a beautiful view does indeed unfold, though this is partly because of the fire that consumed the trees that used to block the view.
From here we descend west to Khirbet Rakit, which has a fine burial cave, and to the Rakit picnic area beside it, a convenient spot for a break and a rest, with water and toilets.
The trail crosses the entrance road to the Yearot HaCarmel Hotel and continues west to the Nahal Oren parking area. On this section the trail descends gently, and we pass the Yishah Caves. On the final section before the parking area, the trail descends steeply, with a short passage between large boulders and a descent to the parking area.
nearby_en: The memorial to the victims of the Carmel fire disaster.
author_en: Omer Shapira, Content Coordinator, Tourism Division, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel.
